source_boundary.preserved_question_intent: Explain common MySQL cases in which an existing index is not usable for the desired lookup or is not selected by the optimizer, especially leftmost-prefix violations and implicit type conversion, while preserving MySQL 8.4 nuances around ranges, LIKE, functional indexes, skip scan and cost-based plan choice.

sources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual §10.3.1 How MySQL Uses Indexes
anchors: MySQL uses indexes for matching rows in WHERE conditions and may choose scans when an index does not reduce the search enough
comparison compatibility including string character set/collation matters for index lookup
multiple-column indexes are usable through leftmost prefixes

sources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual §10.3.6 Multiple-Column Indexes
anchors: an index on (col1,col2,col3) has leftmost prefixes (col1), (col1,col2), and (col1,col2,col3)
predicates starting only from col2 or col2,col3 do not provide the ordinary leftmost-prefix lookup of that composite index

sources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual §10.2.1.2 Range Optimization
anchors: BTREE range access can use LIKE when the pattern does not begin with a wildcard
for multi-part indexes equality-like constraints can extend an interval through additional key parts while a range operator limits how subsequent parts contribute to the same interval
operators such as !=, <>, IS NOT NULL and OR can still participate in range conditions in supported forms
Skip Scan can in some cases exploit a composite index even when the first key part lacks an equality predicate

sources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual §14.3 Type Conversion in Expression Evaluation
anchors: an indexed string column compared with a numeric value cannot use that string-column index for fast lookup because multiple strings can convert to the same numeric value
comparison coercion rules can therefore make the indexed expression unsuitable for direct index lookup

sources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual §10.2.1.23 Avoiding Full Table Scans
anchors: the optimizer can choose a full table scan when a table is small or an indexed predicate is estimated to retrieve a large fraction of rows
ANALYZE TABLE can refresh index statistics used by the optimizer

sources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual §10.8.2 EXPLAIN Output Format and EXPLAIN ANALYZE
anchors: EXPLAIN shows the optimizer's selected access plan
EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and provides actual timing and row information for plan validation

sources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual §15.1.15 CREATE INDEX Statement
anchors: MySQL supports functional key parts in indexes
therefore applying a function to a column is not a timeless rule that indexing is impossible; expression/index matching must be evaluated

claims.text: For an ordinary composite BTREE lookup, predicates that do not preserve a usable leftmost prefix can prevent the expected direct index access, although MySQL features such as Skip Scan mean the interview mnemonic must not be stated as an exception-free optimizer law.
Implicit type conversion can make an indexed expression unusable for fast lookup; MySQL explicitly documents the indexed-string-column versus numeric-value case.

A leading-wildcard LIKE pattern cannot form the same BTREE prefix range as a constant-prefix pattern, while LIKE 'abc%' can participate in range access. Range predicates on a composite index constrain how later key parts contribute to the same interval rather than proving that the whole index is universally unusable.

Wrapping an indexed column in an unmatched expression can defeat the original column-index lookup, but MySQL supports functional key parts, so 'functions always invalidate indexes' is not a correct universal rule.

An index can remain structurally usable yet not be selected because the optimizer estimates a table scan to be cheaper, for example on a small table or a predicate that matches much of the table; statistics influence that decision.
Whether a query actually uses an index is a plan question that should be verified with EXPLAIN and, when appropriate, EXPLAIN ANALYZE rather than inferred only from memorized rules.

writer_constraints: Use 'index not usable for this lookup', 'access path not chosen' or equivalent language instead of implying that the index object itself became invalid.
Cover the frozen entities explicitly: leftmost-prefix behavior and implicit type conversion.
Do not say !=, <>, IS NOT NULL, IN, OR, or range predicates always disable an index; MySQL range optimization can use several of these forms.

Explain that a range condition on an earlier composite-index key part can stop later parts from extending the same lookup interval, while later parts may still be applied for filtering/other optimization depending on the plan.
Distinguish leading-wildcard LIKE such as '%abc' from constant-prefix LIKE such as 'abc%'.
Do not say applying any function necessarily makes indexing impossible; MySQL supports functional key parts and expression matching matters.
Include optimizer cost/selectivity/statistics as a separate reason why a usable index may not be selected.
Recommend EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE and statistics inspection to validate the actual plan.
Do not fabricate table names, row counts, index names, latency improvements or production incidents.
